title: WHEN LOYALTY TO A LEADER BECOMES DISLOYALTY TO CHRIST
paragraphs: WHEN LOYALTY TO A LEADER BECOMES DISLOYALTY TO CHRIST

The most dangerous spiritual betrayal may not begin when you abandon your church. It may begin when you become so loyal to a Christian leader that you stop asking whether you are still loyal to Jesus.
There is a kind of betrayal that does not look like betrayal.
It says, “You don’t understand what he has done for me.”
It whispers, “Don’t touch the Lord’s anointed.”
And sometimes, beneath all that religious language, something frightening has happened almost unnoticed:
Jesus is no longer the One we are protecting most.
That sentence may make some people uncomfortable.

Not because discomfort is automatically conviction, and certainly not because every accusation against a leader is true. Scripture condemns false witness. Scripture commands believers to honor faithful leaders. Scripture teaches respect for those who labor among God’s people.

But Scripture never gives a pastor, preacher, prophet, apostle, teacher, ministry founder, church elder, celebrity Christian, political figure, or spiritual mentor the throne that belongs to Jesus Christ.
And this is where the heart gets exposed.
Because sometimes the person who taught you to follow Jesus can slowly become the person you are following instead of Jesus.
Maybe their preaching reached you during the darkest season of your life.
Maybe their sermons played while you cried alone.
Maybe their ministry helped restore your marriage.
Maybe their teaching brought you back to Scripture.
Maybe they prayed for you when nobody else knew your name.
Maybe they discipled you, believed in you, corrected you, encouraged you, employed you, promoted you, or gave you opportunities you never imagined having.
A contradiction between what was preached publicly and what was practiced privately.
And suddenly, without realizing it, you were no longer asking:
That is the moment loyalty can become dangerous.
Because Christian loyalty is never permission to participate in darkness.
And love does not require blindness.
The apostle Paul gives us words sharp enough to cut through our excuses:
“Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην.”
In context, Paul is defending the divine origin and integrity of the Gospel against distortion. The closing words are devastating:
Paul's question is essentially this: Am I living for human approval, or do I belong to Christ?
Because eventually those allegiances can collide.
And when they do, you discover who actually owns your obedience.
This does not mean Christians should become suspicious, rebellious, cynical people who attack every pastor over disagreements.

The Bible explicitly commands believers to respect faithful spiritual leadership. Hebrews 13:17 speaks seriously about responding to leaders who watch over souls. First Thessalonians 5:12–13 tells believers to recognize and esteem those who labor among them. First Timothy 5:19 warns against casually receiving accusations against an elder.
Biblical Christianity has no room for reckless slander disguised as “discernment.”
Because the same Bible refuses to make leaders untouchable.
First Timothy 5:20 addresses elders who persist in sin and requires public rebuke so that others may fear.
The Bible that teaches honor also teaches accountability.
The Bible that condemns false accusation also condemns covering persistent sin.
The Bible that tells believers to respect leaders never tells believers to worship them.
That balance matters because wounded people often swing between two extremes.
Others refuse to believe any allegation against someone they admire.
Truth does not become false because your enemy said it.
And falsehood does not become true because your favorite preacher said it.
Think about the church in Corinth.
People were forming camps around personalities.
Paul's response was not, “Excellent. Defend my brand.”
“What then is Apollos? What is Paul?”
And then Paul drives the foundation even deeper:
“For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.”
And whenever a ministry begins functioning as though questioning its leader equals questioning God, something has gone terribly wrong.
Whenever protecting an institution becomes more important than protecting wounded people, something has gone wrong.
Whenever reputation matters more than repentance, something has gone wrong.
Whenever “unity” means silence about sin, something has gone wrong.
Whenever someone demands the kind of unquestioning allegiance Scripture reserves for Christ, something has gone wrong.
Because biblical authority is delegated authority.
“All authority has been given to Me…”
Every legitimate Christian leader serves beneath that authority.
Nobody graduates beyond accountability to Jesus.
Nobody becomes too successful to repent.
Nobody gathers enough followers to rewrite Scripture.
Nobody becomes so “anointed” that character stops mattering.
And nobody becomes so useful to the kingdom that God suddenly needs Christians to lie in order to protect them.
God does not need your dishonesty to defend His work.
God does not need your dishonesty to defend His work.
If something is false, reject the falsehood.
If something is unproven, do not present it as fact.
If something is gossip, refuse to spread it.
If someone is being slandered, defend them appropriately.
But if something is demonstrably true, calling truth “an attack” does not transform it into a lie.
Sometimes what people call “protecting the ministry” is actually protecting an image.
There is another scene in Scripture that makes this impossible to escape.
Peter and the apostles are standing before religious authorities.
They have been commanded to stop.
Peitharchein dei Theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
“We must obey God rather than men.”
There comes a moment when obedience to God requires disappointing a human being.
Maybe even a human being you love.
Maybe someone who gave you a platform.
Maybe someone whose approval became part of your identity.
And this is where discipleship becomes painfully personal.
Would you still obey Jesus if obedience cost you access to the leader you admire?
Would you still tell the truth if telling it cost you your position?
Would you still refuse wrongdoing if everyone around you called your refusal “disloyal”?
Would you still follow Christ if your spiritual family misunderstood you?
Would you still stand with Scripture if the person who originally taught you Scripture abandoned what it says?
That is harder than sharing inspirational verses online.
Because sometimes carrying a cross means losing the approval of people whose approval once meant everything to you.
And before we become self-righteous, there is another side of this.
Perhaps somebody calls you pastor, teacher, mentor, elder, leader, mother, father, discipler, or spiritual adviser.
Their loyalty is not yours to possess.
Teach them enough Scripture that they can recognize when even you are wrong.
Build people who love Christ more than they love you.
Do not use Scripture to frighten people into silence.
John the Baptist understood something that modern Christian celebrity culture desperately needs to recover.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
That is leadership in the kingdom.
A faithful preacher should leave you increasingly captivated by Christ, not increasingly incapable of imagining Christianity without the preacher.
And perhaps this is where some readers feel an old wound opening.
Then discovered something that devastated you.
Maybe the scandal did more than damage your opinion of a person.
A fallen messenger does not make a faithful Christ unfaithful.
Your faith was never supposed to stand on the perfection of the person who introduced you to Him.
Jesus did not say, “Follow My representatives as long as they never disappoint you.”
Maybe somebody failed you so badly that you walked away from church.
Maybe you walked away from prayer.
Maybe you cannot hear a sermon without suspicion anymore.
Maybe the name of a ministry triggers memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe you feel foolish because you defended someone you later discovered you should not have defended.
Maybe you repeated things that were not true.
Maybe you attacked someone who was telling the truth.
Maybe you stayed silent because you were afraid.
Maybe you knew something was wrong and convinced yourself that protecting “God’s work” justified looking away.
Then there is something you desperately need to hear.
Failure is not the end of your story.
Peter knew what it meant to choose self-preservation over loyalty to Jesus.
He swore he would never deny Christ.
The sound of discovering that the person you thought you were was not the person pressure revealed you to be.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But Jesus was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, beside a charcoal fire, Jesus restored the disciple who had denied Him.
Not pretending Peter never denied Him.
Not rewriting history to protect Peter’s reputation.
Grace tells the truth about the scandal and then demonstrates that the scandal does not get the final word.
Maybe you defended the wrong person.
Maybe you participated in a culture of silence.
Maybe you were the leader who manipulated loyalty.
Maybe pride has made confession feel impossible because too many people think highly of you.
Come down from the pedestal voluntarily before the pedestal becomes your prison.
There is room at the cross.
There is blood sufficient for hypocrites.
For people who defended what they should have confronted.
For people who confronted things with cruelty instead of love.
For the betrayer who genuinely repents.
This is why Christianity can tell the truth about scandal without surrendering to despair.
Because our hope was never human perfection.
Our hope is a crucified and risen Savior.
Jesus Christ took sinners' guilt upon Himself at Calvary.
And He does not merely expose sin.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
If your leader obeys Christ, encourage them.
But never give them what belongs only to Jesus.
And if the terrible day comes when loyalty to a human leader requires disobedience to Christ, you already know where a disciple must stand.
And perhaps somebody you know needs to read this before loyalty carries them somewhere their conscience has already warned them not to go.
And if this exposed something in you, do not hide behind a reaction button.

Your confession does not have to contain anybody's name. Do not turn the comments into a courtroom or gossip thread. Let it become something better—a place where people point one another back to Christ.
Because convictions that feel obvious today become expensive when relationships are on the line.
Support Christian work only insofar as it faithfully points people toward Him.
Never replace Jesus with Gospel Warrior either.
If we ever contradict Christ, choose Christ.
If your favorite preacher contradicts Christ, choose Christ.
If your denomination contradicts Christ, choose Christ.
If your closest friend asks you to compromise Christ, choose Christ.
If choosing Christ costs applause, choose Christ.
Because one day every platform will disappear.
Every ministry name will pass from history.
Every human reputation will finally be stripped of its mythology.
And only One King will still be standing.
Forgive where there is genuine repentance.
And never confuse loyalty to a servant with allegiance to the King.
Because the most heartbreaking thing would not be discovering that the leader you defended was wrong.
It would be discovering that somewhere along the way, while fighting desperately to remain loyal to them, you became disloyal to Christ.
Never hold a leader so tightly that you have to loosen your grip on Jesus.
